title: Towards Diffeomorphism-Equivariant Neural Networks via Canonicalization
claim: A model should respond predictably to input transformations: outputs transform correspondingly (equivariance) or stay unchanged (invariance) under the same deformation.
layout: 2 panels, commutative-diagram grid, left-to-right and top-down, g arrows
description: Two panels separated by a vertical line. Panel (a), diffeomorphism equivariance, is a 2x2 grid in the style of a commutative diagram. The top row shows a chest X-ray labeled Input, with an arrow labeled 'Segmentation f_θ' to a yellow-on-purple lung mask labeled Output. The bottom row shows the same X-ray, warped and labeled Transformed Input, with the same segmentation arrow to a correspondingly warped mask labeled Output of Transformed Input. Vertical arrows labeled g link top to bottom. Panel (b), diffeomorphism invariance, shows an MNIST digit 8 and its stretched, deformed version linked by a vertical g arrow. Two diagonal 'Classification f_θ' arrows from the two digits converge on one boxed output, 'genus two'. The eye goes first to the colorful images and arrows. Captions (a) and (b) sit below each panel.
caption: Examples of (a) diffeomorphism equivariance in lung image (RSUA, 2023) segmentation and (b) diffeomorphism invariance in predictions of topological invariants in MNIST (LeCun et al., 1998). Applying a diffeomorphism g ∈D(X) to the input should result in a correspondingly transformed segmentation output, i.e., fθ(g · x) = g · fθ(x), and preserve the classification, i.e., fθ(g · x) = fθ(x).
abstract: Incorporating group symmetries via equivariance into neural networks has emerged as a robust approach for improving efficiency and overcoming the data requirements of modern deep learning. While most existing approaches, such as group convolutions and averaging-based methods, focus on compact, finite, or low-dimensional groups with linear actions, this work explores how equivariance can be extended to infinite-dimensional groups. We propose a strategy designed to induce diffeomorphism equivariance in pre-trained neural networks via energy-based canonicalization. Formulating equivariance as an optimization problem allows us to access the rich toolbox of already established differentiable image registration methods. Empirical results on segmentation and classification tasks confirm that our approach achieves approximate equivariance and generalizes to unseen transformations without relying on extensive data augmentation or retraining.
